title: ZuckOff Is a Free App That Sees Meta Glasses Before They See You
gist: A Polish developer built ZuckOff, a free app that fingerprints the Bluetooth signals of smart glasses to alert users when Ray-Ban Meta, Oakley Meta, or Snap Spectacles are nearby. It has passed 5,000 iOS downloads since August amid rising backlash over covert filming, with roughly 7 million pairs of Meta smart glasses sold in 2025 and recording-indicator LEDs proving easy to defeat.

insights.claim: A 30-year-old Polish developer built a free mobile app that uses Bluetooth detection to tell a user whether a pair of smart glasses is in the room with them.
insights.speaker: Megan Tomos
insights.so_what: Consumer counter-surveillance tooling is now a one-person build, meaning every ambient-sensing device invites a detector product.
insights.quote: uses a Bluetooth detection system to tell you whether there is a pair of smart glasses in the room with you

insights.claim: The detection method works by recording the Bluetooth signals broadcast by various smart glasses models to build a digital fingerprint for each, flagging when a unique identifier matches a manufacturer identifier.
insights.speaker: Megan Tomos
insights.so_what: Manufacturer identifiers in Bluetooth advertising packets are an unpatched leak that lets third parties inventory nearby devices.
insights.quote: building a digital fingerprint for each of them

insights.claim: The app was downloaded by more than 5,000 people on Apple's App Store since its August launch and 1,000 times on the Google Play Store.
insights.speaker: Megan Tomos
insights.so_what: Adoption is small in absolute terms but demonstrates real latent demand for defensive privacy tools against wearables.
insights.quote: the app has reportedly been downloaded by more than 5,000 people on Apple’s App Store

insights.claim: Basic scanning is free while a $25 Pro version adds history logging, CSV data export, a homescreen widget, and continuous background monitoring that alerts even with the screen off.
insights.speaker: Megan Tomos
insights.so_what: A working freemium monetization model for counter-surveillance suggests the category can sustain independent developers.
insights.quote: there is also a ZuckOff Pro version available to purchase for $25

insights.claim: The app is difficult for the glasses maker to legally take down because it does not interfere with the signals the glasses send, only passively reads them.
insights.speaker: Megan Tomos
insights.so_what: Passive observation of public radio broadcasts is a defensible legal posture that manufacturers cannot easily litigate away.
insights.quote: The app is also a pretty difficult thing for Meta to legally take down, since it isn’t interfering with the signals being sent by the glasses.

insights.claim: The tool cannot say whether nearby glasses are actively recording or who is wearing them, only rough proximity from signal strength, which turns an invisible problem into a partially visible one.
insights.speaker: Megan Tomos
insights.so_what: Partial visibility is the honest ceiling of passive detection; it raises awareness without resolving consent.
insights.quote: which turns an invisible problem into a partially visible one, which at the very least is worth something until legislators take protective action

themes.theme: Smart glasses backlash and the failing LED

insights.claim: Unsolicited filming with smart glasses is a growing public safety concern, with people wearing them to film their dates and venues including schools and cinemas increasingly banning them outright.
insights.speaker: Megan Tomos
insights.so_what: Venue-level bans are the first commercial friction point for smart glasses adoption, ahead of any regulation.
insights.quote: Venues like schools and cinemas are increasingly banning their usage outright.

insights.claim: A BBC investigation in January traced dozens of accounts posting content of women filmed in public by smart glasses without consent, including one video exposing a 21-year-old woman's face and phone number that amassed over 1.3 million views.
insights.speaker: Megan Tomos
insights.so_what: Documented viral harm gives regulators a concrete evidentiary basis for wearable-camera rules.
insights.quote: One video posted a 21-year-old woman’s face and phone number and amassed over 1.3 million views.

insights.claim: Recording indicator lights on these glasses have proven fairly easy to defeat with simple hardware hacks, allowing a growing number of wearers to record undetected.
insights.speaker: Megan Tomos
insights.so_what: The single privacy safeguard the industry points to is physically defeatable, which invalidates the consent model built on it.
insights.quote: The recording indicator lights on these glasses have proven fairly easy to defeat with simple hardware hacks

insights.claim: Roughly 7 million pairs of Meta's smart glasses were sold in 2025.
insights.speaker: Megan Tomos
insights.so_what: Installed base at that scale means bystander exposure is now a mass-market condition, not an edge case.
insights.quote: Roughly 7 million pairs of Meta’s smart glasses were sold in 2025.

insights.claim: In July the manufacturer announced a software update that detects when an LED has been physically tampered with or destroyed and blocks filming with those cameras.
insights.speaker: Megan Tomos
insights.so_what: Vendors are patching hardware tampering in software, an arms race that detection apps will keep pressuring.

insights.claim: A contradiction sits at the heart of the product: the company's CTO says the camera was designed to be noticed by people around you, yet one of the product's key commercial propositions is that the camera doesn't look like a camera.
insights.speaker: Megan Tomos
insights.so_what: Discreetness sells the product and undermines its safety story simultaneously, which is why regulation rather than design will settle it.
insights.quote: This is despite the fact that one of the product's key commercial propositions is that the camera doesn't look like a camera.

insights.claim: California and other territories have taken steps to criminalize disabling the recording light or recording people without their consent.
insights.speaker: Megan Tomos
insights.so_what: State-level criminalization of tamper and nonconsensual recording is the emerging regulatory template for wearable cameras.
